planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring at soil level in full sun and well-drained soil on the northern Plains or other cold, dry climates where Ogallala's heritage shines.

directions: Ogallala was released jointly by the University of Nebraska's North Platte Experiment Station and the USDA, bred by Glenn Viehmeyer over roughly 25 years of breeding that incorporated the wild Rocky Mountain strawberry (Fragaria ovalis) crossed with 'Fairfax' for cold hardiness and drought tolerance. Plant crowns at soil level in full sun; this everbearer tolerates open, exposed winters on the northern Great Plains with little to no mulch and shrugs off dry spells better than most modern cultivars. It produces a solid spring flush of medium, dark-red, tangy-flavored berries followed by a lighter but steady crop into fall. Remove runners and renovate beds periodically to keep plantings vigorous, since productivity can decline in heavier, poorly-drained soils.
sources: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension Circular EC58-1202
North Dakota State University Extension — Strawberries

planting.note: Plant dormant tip-layered canes in early spring; Dundee tolerates heavier, less-well-drained soils better than most black raspberries, though canes can be damaged by wind.

directions: Dundee is a 1927 Geneva, New York black raspberry cultivar (a Smith1 x Palmer cross) valued for its productive, vigorous, hardy plants and tolerance of soils that are a bit heavier or less well-drained than most black raspberries can stand. Tip-prune new primocanes in midsummer to force the lateral branching that bears next year's fruit, and plant in a sheltered spot since canes are relatively easily damaged by strong wind. Fruit is dull black rather than glossy, but of good classic black-raspberry flavor and quality. Remove spent floricanes after harvest to keep anthracnose and other cane diseases in check.
sources: USDA-ARS genetic diversity research on black raspberry germplasm
University of Maine Cooperative Extension — Raspberry and Blackberry Varieties

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tips in early spring in full sun; Huron ripens a bit later than most black raspberries, extending the harvest window.

directions: Huron is a vigorous black raspberry cultivar grown for its big, glossy, high-quality black fruit that ripens somewhat later than Bristol or Cumberland, which helps spread out the harvest in a mixed planting. Grow it as a typical black raspberry: tip-prune summer primocanes to encourage branching, provide full sun and well-drained soil, and remove spent floricanes promptly after fruiting to limit disease carryover. Expect a concentrated but later midsummer crop with good flavor for fresh eating, jam, and freezing. Good air circulation between hills reduces pressure from cane diseases common to the genus.
sources: University of Maine Cooperative Extension — Raspberry and Blackberry Varieties

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring; Allen was selected for strong disease resistance, making it a dependable choice where anthracnose and cane blights are common.

directions: Allen was introduced by the Geneva, New York Experiment Station in 1963 (a Bristol x Cumberland cross) and remains notable among black raspberries for its consistent productivity and strong resistance to common cane diseases. Grow it like other black raspberries: plant in full sun, tip-prune new canes in midsummer to force fruiting laterals, and cut spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest. The large berries carry strong, classic black raspberry flavor that holds up well for both fresh eating and preserves. Its disease resistance makes it a good candidate for organic or low-spray home plantings.
sources: USDA-ARS genetic diversity research on black raspberry germplasm

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring; Canby's nearly spine-free canes make hand-harvest and maintenance noticeably easier than thorny cultivars.

directions: Canby was released in 1953 by the USDA and the Oregon Agricultural Experiment Station (now Oregon State University), bred by George Waldo, and is prized for its tall, nearly thornless canes, which make trellising, pruning, and picking far more pleasant than with spiny red raspberries. Train canes to a two-wire trellis in full sun and well-drained soil; fruit is medium to large, firm, bright red, and well regarded for flavor in both fresh eating and preserves. It was bred for the Pacific Northwest and performs best there, with fruiting buds that can suffer in severe cold farther inland. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Raspberry Cultivars for the Pacific Northwest
University of Maine Cooperative Extension — Raspberry and Blackberry Varieties

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring; Newburgh is an old, very hardy New York cultivar valued as a parent of many modern raspberries.

directions: Newburgh is a historic hardy red raspberry bred in New York in the 1920s and still referenced in extension cultivar guides for its reliable winter survival and partial resistance to common cane diseases and root rot. Canes are tall with relatively few spines but only moderate vigor, so give plants full sun and fertile, well-drained soil and avoid crowding. Fruit is medium-sized and light red with good flavor, though berries can be somewhat crumbly and may ripen unevenly within a cluster. Its main garden value today is extreme cold hardiness for northern growers rather than the heaviest yields.
sources: University of Maine Cooperative Extension — Raspberry and Blackberry Varieties
Oregon State University Extension — Circular of Information 533

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring on a trellis; Octavia fruits late in the floricane season, bridging the gap before fall-fruiting types begin.

directions: Octavia was bred at East Malling Research in the UK (a Glen Ample x EM 5928/114 cross) as a late floricane-fruiting red raspberry that extends the summer raspberry season well into late summer, bridging the gap before primocane-fruiting (fall) types take over. Train canes to a trellis in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; berries are large, firm, and easy to pick cleanly from the plug, with very good flavor for fresh eating. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to the sturdiest growth each spring. It suits gardeners who want to stretch the raspberry harvest window without switching to a different fruiting type.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring; Jaclyn is a primocane (everbearing) type patented out of a University of Maryland breeding program.

directions: Jaclyn is a primocane-fruiting red raspberry developed through a University of Maryland breeding program and patented (US Plant Patent PP15,647) for its large, firm berries and good disease resistance. Because it fruits on first-year canes, it can be mowed to the ground every winter for simple, low-maintenance pruning, or managed as a double-cropper by leaving floricanes for an early summer harvest in addition to the fall primocane crop. Plant in full sun with consistent moisture during fruit set, since primocane types benefit from even watering through the extended late-summer to fall harvest window. Its everbearing habit suits home gardeners who want fresh raspberries from late summer through the first hard frost.
sources: US Plant Patent PP15,647 (University of Maryland)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring in well-drained soil; Cascade Bounty was bred specifically for strong tolerance to Phytophthora root rot.

directions: Cascade Bounty was released jointly by Washington State University, Oregon State University, the University of Idaho, and USDA-ARS (US Plant Patent PP18,246) specifically for its outstanding tolerance to Phytophthora root rot, a major limiting disease for red raspberries in wetter climates. Train the floricane-fruiting canes to a trellis in full sun; even so, it still benefits from the well-drained soil or raised beds typically recommended for raspberries, since root rot tolerance reduces risk rather than eliminating the need for good drainage. Fruit is medium-sized and bright red with fair flavor, making it more of a reliable workhorse than a flavor showcase. It is a good option for gardeners in heavier or poorly-drained soils where other red raspberries have struggled.
sources: US Plant Patent PP18,246 (Washington State University Research Foundation)
Washington State University / Oregon State University small fruit breeding programs
